ORGANIC CHEMISTRY
Stereodivergent access to non-natural a-amino acids
via enantio- and Z/E-selective catalysis
Panpan Li1, En Zheng 2, Guanlin Li 1, Yicong Luo 1, Xiaohong Huo 1, Shengming Ma 2,3*, Wanbin Zhang 1*
The precise control ofZ and E configurations of the carbon-carbon double bond in alkene synthesis
has long been a fundamental challenge in synthetic chemistry, even more pronounced when simultaneously
striving to achieve enantioselectivity [(Z,R), (Z,S), (E,R), (E,S)]. Moreover, enantiopure non-naturala-amino
acids are highly sought after in organic and medicinal chemistry. In this study, we report a ligand-controlled
stereodivergent synthesis of non-naturala-quaternary amino acids bearingtrisubstituted alkene moieties
in high yields with excellent enantioselectivity andZ/E selectivities. This success is achieved through
a palladium/copper–cocatalyzed three-component assembly of readily available aryl iodides, allenes, and
aldimine esters by simply tuning the chiral ligands of the palladium and copper catalysts.

wenty proteinogenic amino acids pave
the foundation of the origin and evolu-
tion of life. Thus, entries to optically active
non-naturala-amino acids have numer-
ous applications to the study on the
pivotal role of amino acids in the life sciences,
drug development, protein engineering, and
biomaterial research (1–9). In this domain, the
incorporation of latent (bio)orthogonal reac-
tive alkene functional groups into a-amino
acids not only enriches their biological proper-
ties but also establishes a versatile platform that
enables multiple transformations for generat-
ing structurally diverse non-natural a-amino
acids (Fig. 1A) ( 10–14). It is known that mol-
ecules with different stereochemistry ( Z and
E, R and S) exhibit distinctly different biolog-
ical activities ( 15, 16). Therefore, the devel-
opment of an efficient and general catalytic
strategy for the stereodivergent synthesis of
chiral non-naturala-amino acids bearing stereo-
defined alkene moieties [(Z,R), (Z,S), (E,R), (E,S)]
is highly desirable. In asymmetric catalysis, chi-

ing different types of chiral entities. However,
achieving full stereocontrol over both the cen-
tral chirality and C=C bond configuration con-
tinues to pose a challenge.
The precise control of both Z and E con-
figurations of C=C bonds has long been a per-
sistent challenge in organic chemistry because
of thermodynamic and kinetic issues (17, 18).
Among the limited methods that exist (19–24),
chemistry involving p-allyl metal intermedi-
ates may, in principle, offer a direct and ele-
gant strategy for the selective preparation of
Z-o r E-olefinic compounds bearing chiral
centers (Fig. 1B) (25–37
). The configuration of
the resulting alkenes is primarily determined
by the selective formation of syn-o r anti-
p-allyl metal intermediates, as well as by the
selective capture of these intermediates by
prochiral nucleophiles.For 1-monosubstituted
p-allyl-metal intermediates, the relative ther-
modynamic stabilities of the intermediates
contribute to the dominance of syn-p-allyl-
metal intermediates, and chiralE-disubstituted
olefinic compounds [( E,R)o r( E,S)] are the
predominant products (Fig. 1B, left) ( 25–35).
However, capturing the thermodynamically
unstable anti-p-allyl-metal intermediates with
prochiral nucleophiles for the generation of chi-
ral Z-disubstituted olefinic compounds [(Z,R)
or (Z,S)] presents a great challenge owing to
unfavorable R/[TM/L*] strain, and advance-

or aryl group; TM, transition metal; L*, chiral
ligand) (Fig. 1B, right). Although transition
metal–catalyzedZ-retentive allylic substitution
reactions have been realized ( 36, 37), asym-
metric versions have only recently been reported
by You ’s group ( 38, 39). By contrast, for 1,2-
disubstituted p-allyl-metal intermediates, R/
[TM/L*] strain and 1,2-steric repulsion are
present in theanti-a n dsyn-intermediates, re-
spectively (Fig. 1C). As a result, the anti-a n d
syn-p-allyl-metal intermediates are often ener-
getically close, adding extra complexities to the
control ofZ or E selectivity in the to-be-formed
trisubstituted alkenes (
40, 41). To date, the di-
vergent synthesis of both Z- and E-alkenes
through the selective formation and capture of
anti-o r syn-p-allyl metal intermediates remains
an elusive goal. Furthermore, this task becomes
more challenging for the full stereodivergent
synthesis of all four stereoisomers of enantio-
pureZ-a n dE-trisubstituted alkenes [(Z,R), (Z,S),
(E,R), ( E,S)] from just a single set of starting
materials.
Allenes manifest distinctive properties and
reactivities because of their cumulated diene
system (42–44). In this regard, a palladium-
catalyzed carbopalladation process of allenes
with aryl iodides represents a direct approach
to generate the 1,2-disubstitutedsyn-o r anti-
p-allyl-palladium intermediates, albeit with
limited control over their distributions and
reactivities (45–47). On the basis of our efforts
in allene chemistry and bimetallic catalysis
(48–51), we envisaged that the thermody-
namic stabilities of the syn-a n d anti-p-allyl-
palladium intermediates and their reactivities
toward prochiral nucleophiles could be com-
prehensively regulated by using two chiral
catalysts. Here, we report a Pd/Cu synergistic
catalytic system that enables the stereodi-
vergent synthesis of enantiopure non-natural
a-quaternary amino acids bearing Z-a n d
E-trisubstituted alkene moieties through a
three-component assembly with aryl iodides,
simple allenes, and a-amino acid–derived al-
dimine esters (Fig. 1D). Two chiral catalysts
could exert comprehensive stereocontrol over
the configurations of the C=C bond and chi-
ral center. This modular catalytic protocol
allows access to all four stereoisomers of non-
natural a
-quaternary amino acids bearing tri-
substituted alkene moieties in high yields
with excellent enantioselectivities andZ/E se-
lectivities from the same set of readily avail-
able starting materials with judicious ligand
combinations.

Mechanistic investigations
To gain insights into the mechanism of this
ligand-controlled stereodivergent process, sev-
eral mechanistic experiments were conducted.
At first, the reactions were monitored over
time under the E- and Z-selective conditions,
respectively (figs. S2 and S3). There was no
change in the E/Z ratios and e.e. values of the
products ( E,R)-6b and ( Z,R)-6b as the reac-
tion proceeded. These results suggest that the
E/Z isomerization of trisubstituted alkenes
does not occur, thus further supporting the
ligand control for stereoselectivity in our dual-
catalytic system ( 52, 53). To understand the
different behaviors of L2- and L3-ligated
p-allyl-Pd intermediates, additional experiments
were performed. In general, the characteriza-
tion of anti-o r syn-p-allyl-Pd complexes could
provide valuable information for further un-
derstanding the origin of theE or Z selectivity
(39, 54). Fortunately, theanti-p-allyl-Pd/L3 in-
termediate 17 was successfully obtained as a
single isomer, which was determined by x-ray
diffraction analysis (Fig. 5A). No isomerization
of this anti-p-allyl-Pd/L3 complex was ob-
served at 50°C, even over 36 hours (fig. S4).
Then, the stoichiometric complex 17 was re-
acted with the aldimine ester3a using the Cu/
L1 catalyst, affording the product 4a with
nearly complete E selectivity (Fig. 5A). Subse-
quently, pure ( Z)- and ( E)-2-aryl-substituted
cinnamyl carbonates 18 and 19 were exam-
ined under standard E-selective conditions,
which could, in principle, initially generate the
anti-a n d syn-p-allyl-Pd/ L3 intermediates
through the ionization process, respectively
(Fig. 5B). Regardless of whether ( Z)-18/19 or
(E)-18/19 were used, the E-selective products
(E)-6b/20 were predominant. Moreover, both
(Z)- and ( E)-19 were reacted with a stoichio-
metric amount of the Pd0/L3 catalyst, and the
reactions were monitored by 31Pa n d 19Fn u -
clear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy
(figs. S5 and S6). It was observed that ( Z)-19
preferentially generated the anti-p-allyl-Pd/
L3 intermediate, which increased in concen-
tration over time. By contrast, (E)-19 initially
formed thesyn-p-allyl-Pd/L3intermediate, which
readily converted into the anti-p-allyl-Pd/L3
intermediate. These results indicate that the
formation of theanti-p-allyl-Pd/L3 is thermo-
dynamically favored.
To gain a deeper understanding of the origin
of the observed E selectivity in the current
Pd/L3 catalytic system, kinetic experiments
and density functional theory (DFT) calcu-
lations were conducted. First, the migratory
insertion process of the allene moiety into
the aryl-Pd bond was examined through 31P
NMR monitoring experiments involving the
reaction of the allene with stoichiometric
aryl-PdII species (figs. S7 and S8). The results
showed that the anti-p-allyl-Pd/L3 species
was preferentially formed without isomeri-
zation, indicating that this species also acts
as a kinetic intermediate. Additionally, a ki-
netic study on the concentration of the copper
catalyst revealed a zero-order rate dependence,
suggesting that the nucleophilic attack process
is not the rate-determining step (fig. S15). These
experimental results imply that the migratory
insertion is the E-selective stereocontrol step.
Subsequently, DFT computations for all eight
complete reaction pathways were investigated
(fig. S24). The free-energy profiles of two fav-
ored pathways for the formation of E-a n d
Z-selective products are shown in Fig. 5C. Both
pathways begin with the Pd 0/L3 complex
IM-(E)-1, followed by oxidative addition via
TS-(E)-1a, forming the aryl-Pd/ L3-I species
IM-(E)-2a. A ligand-exchange process between
IM-(E)-2a and allene 2b then occurs, afford-
ing IM-(E)-3ab and IM-(E)-3ac.S u b s e q u e n t
migratory insertion inIM-(E)-3abandIM-(E)-
3ac generatesIM-(anti)-4ab and IM-(syn)-
4ac, respectively. The calculations reveal that the
energy barrier for the formation ofIM-(anti)-
4ab is obviously lower than that for the for-
mation of theIM-(syn)-4acby 10.48 kcal/mol
[TS-(E)-3abversusTS-(E)-3ac], owing to the
considerable steric hindrance between the
allene and ligand moieties inTS-(E)-3ac (fig.
S28). Lastly, the copper-chelated nucleophileNu
attacks the cationic intermediate IM-(anti)-
4ab via TS-(anti)-4ab, leading to the major
product ( E)-6b. The DFT data are in good
agreement with the experimental results. The
above experimental and computational results
suggest that the migratory insertion step is the
E-selective stereocontrol step, which preferen-
tially generates the thermodynamically and
kinetically favoredanti-p-allyl-Pd/L3 interme-
diate IM-(anti)-4ab. The cationic interme-
diate IM-(anti)-4ab c a nb ed i r e c t l yc a p t u r e d
by the nucleophile to deliver the E-product.

TS-(syn)-4h reveals that the stronger at-
tractive energies and lower distortion ener-
gies present in TS-(syn)-4h contribute to the
favored Z-product (fig. S33). All these results
indicate that selective nucleophilic attack to the
syn-p-allyl-Pd/L2 intermediate is theZ-selective
stereocontrol step, and a specific pathway for
the Z selectivity is proposed as follows: Both
anti-a n dsyn-p-allyl-Pd/L2 intermediates could
be formed by means of the migratory insertion
of the allene moiety into the aryl-Pd bond. The
anti-p-allyl-Pd/L2 intermediate is then con-
verted into thesyn-p-allyl-Pd/
L2 intermediate
through anh3-h1-h3 process, which is captured
by the nucleophile to deliver the Z-product.
In addition, control experiments were con-
ducted to elucidate the roles of the chiral pal-
ladium and copper catalysts in the observed
Z/E selectivity and enantioselectivity (table
S3). The results demonstrate that the chiral
copper catalyst predominantly controls the
enantioselectivity for both Pd/L2 and Pd/L3

alkene configuration and point chirality has
been realized through synergistic dual chiral
metal catalysis. This study not only addresses
a long-standing challenge in p-allyl metal
chemistry for stereocontrol over bothZ and E
configurations of C=C bonds but also provides
a potentially general strategy for the stereo-

Editor’s summary
Adaptable control over the disposition of groups at each end of a carbon-carbon double bond remains a challenge in
chemical synthesis. In the E configuration, the largest groups are diagonally opposed, whereas in the Z configuration,
they’re on the same side. Li et al. paired up copper and palladium catalysts to deliver either E- or Z-configured double
bonds in unnatural amino acids, depending on the ligand choice. The reaction is also highly enantioselective at the
quaternary alpha carbon stereocenter. —Jake S. Yeston
